name: Ergonomic setup (monitor at eye level)
lead: An ergonomic desk setup with the monitor at eye level is a posture practice in which people raise the screen so the head stays upright rather than tilting down. In posture and looksmaxxing communities it is described as a way to avoid so-called tech neck, a forward-head position associated with the neck and jawline, so that a person's neck line, profile and carriage look better after years of desk work.

The practice has a long institutional pedigree. Ergonomics is the scientific discipline that studies interactions between people and the systems they work in, aiming to improve well-being and performance; the term was used by Wojciech Jastrzebowski in 1857 and revived in English in 1949.[1][2] Workplace-safety guidance from the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) gives concrete numbers for monitor placement, and it is this mainstream advice that the appearance communities borrow.[7]

Wikipedia's article on forward head posture says laptops, tablets and phones cannot be set up ergonomically because screen and keyboard are joined, so users hunch over them for hours, increasing load on the neck.[5] No trial of monitor height specifically, nor any study of appearance outcomes, has been published.
infobox: Top of screen at or slightly below eye level; 50-100 cm distance (OSHA) [7]

paras: Ergonomic guidance generally emphasizes neutral body postures, avoiding awkward static positions, and fitting the work setup to the person.[1] Monitor-at-eye-level is a commonly repeated workstation tip, often paired with an external keyboard for laptops. Wikipedia notes that adjustable furniture such as sit-stand desks, along with training, breaks and assessments, are typical workplace measures.[2]

In practice people achieve the height with an adjustable monitor arm or stand, a stack of books, or a laptop riser combined with a separate keyboard and mouse. The aim is to keep the ears roughly over the shoulders and the eyes looking slightly downward at the top of the screen rather than the head hanging forward.

OSHA's computer-workstation guidance says the top of the screen should be at or slightly below eye level, with the centre of the screen about 15 to 20 degrees below horizontal eye level, and that a monitor set too high forces the head to tilt back.[7] It recommends a viewing distance of roughly 20 to 40 inches (50 to 100 cm), a monitor directly in front of the user, and a head, neck and torso that face forward, noting that prolonged side-turning or backward tilting strains neck muscles.[7] For people who wear bifocals, who tend to tilt the head back, it suggests lowering the monitor, raising the chair or using single-vision computer lenses.[7]

This guidance means that 'eye level' in practice refers to the top edge of the screen, not the middle, which is one reason community posts and workplace advice sometimes describe slightly different heights.[7]

Forward head posture is described as the head sitting in front of the shoulders with the chin poking out, with a more pronounced upper-back curve.[5] Wikipedia lists dentists, surgeons, hairdressers and people who spend long hours on devices among those affected, and describes a 'swan-necking' pattern in which the chin juts forward.[5] The article says hunching increases the leverage of the head on the spine and links the rise in neck and upper-back pain to portable devices.[5] A 2019 meta-analysis cited there found a link between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not adolescents.[5]

The appearance rationale proposed in posture and looksmaxxing circles is that a head held forward makes the neck look shorter, the chin and submental area look softer and the upper back look rounder, whereas a stacked head and neck presents a cleaner jaw-to-neck line in profile photographs. Commercial wellness pages make similar claims about double chins, but these are marketing statements rather than published studies, and clinicians note that a double chin can also reflect body fat, genetics or hormones.

Wikipedia lists treatments including posture work, strengthening of the mid-back and deep neck flexors, stretching and ergonomic changes such as regular breaks, and notes parts of that article rest on primary sources.[5]

Wikipedia's computer vision syndrome article lists neck pain among symptoms, names poor sitting position and improper viewing distance as contributing personal factors, and describes the 20-20-20 rule of looking at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes.[6] It gives no specific monitor-height guidance.[6]

Tools such as the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), published in 1993, score neck, trunk and upper limb postures to flag work-related upper limb disorder risk.[3] A meta-analysis of surgeons and interventionalists found high prevalence of work-related musculoskeletal disorders in that group, reflecting sustained neck-flexed postures.[4] Evidence on workstation changes is mixed: Wikipedia reports that several studies of new workstations found improved well-being while many others found no marked health improvement.[2]
No studies found testing monitor height for appearance outcomes. General ergonomics research on musculoskeletal symptoms exists, as described above.[2][3][4]

card.aka: Monitor at eye level, desk ergonomics
card.note: No trials of monitor height and appearance outcomes exist.

quick.overview:
This practice means raising your monitor so your head stays upright instead of tilting down. People discuss it as a way to avoid tech neck.
Ergonomics research focuses on workplace musculoskeletal symptoms. Evidence on workstation changes is mixed and nothing reviewed tests appearance.
quick.mechanism: The idea is that a neutral head position reduces sustained neck flexion and strain, and posture tools like RULA score neck angle as a risk factor.
quick.risks: No notable risks are described. Practice here is a low-cost workstation adjustment.

chain: Screen raised so the gaze is level
Head stays stacked over the shoulders instead of drifting forward
Less sustained neck flexion and forward-head position
Neater neck and jaw profile and more upright carriage
angle.text: Practitioners raise the monitor so the head rests upright during long sessions at a desk. The look-related aim is to avoid a forward-head posture that makes the chin jut and the neck appear shorter.
